gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Victrola's own US store sells the Hi-Res Onyx today (2026-11-13) for $199.99, down from $399.99. That is $99 under the $299 AT-LP70XBT that ChatGPT called 'best overall value'. The Onyx has aptX Adaptive and a VM95E cartridge where the LP70XBT has a VM95C. What you give up is that the Onyx is manual: you lower the tonearm by hand.
standout_why: Turntableverse is the top uncited result, last checked 3 Nov 2026. It lists Sony PS-LX3BT, AT-LP70XBT, Pro-Ject E1 BT, AT-LP120XBT-USB and PS-LX310BT, and no Victrola model at any price. I could not read the two cited pages, What Hi-Fi's Bluetooth list and Louder's best record players: WebFetch returned only their titles and my curl calls were not approved. So I can't rule out that they mention the Onyx. Even if they do, What Hi-Fi's list is dated 16 Oct and Louder's 2 Sep 2025, so neither can carry today's $199.99 price. ChatGPT's own prices are also out of date at the retailer it showed: Sony PS-LX3BT is $399.99 at Turntable Lab, not $349.99, and JBL Spinner BT is $439.95, not $349.95.
decides: The finding splits the pick by how the shopper wants to play records. If they want push-button automatic play, the AT-LP70XBT at $299 still wins: it is fully automatic, $100 under the PS-LX3BT at Turntable Lab, and $140 under the JBL Spinner BT. If they will lower the arm by hand, the Victrola Hi-Res Onyx at $199.99 costs less than the AT-LP60XBT ($259) and still has aptX Adaptive, a VM95E cartridge, a removable headshell and an auto-stop you can switch off. The Hi-Res Carbon at $249.99 (list $599.99) adds an Ortofon 2M Red. ChatGPT's 'Under $200' budget chip had no real candidate; the Onyx fills it.
